title: Good Culture Is the Biggest Productivity Hack, Not AI
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Drawing on 13 years in engineering leadership, the author argues that the current fixation on AI tools and productivity multipliers is misdirected: culture, not tooling, is the real productivity lever, and AI amplifies whatever culture already exists rather than replacing the need for one. The piece identifies two specific executive behaviors that quietly destroy culture — declaring that AI means the company 'doesn't need as many people,' and panicking over competitors' reported 10x AI gains and blaming staff for not matching them — and explains both through Conway's Law, arguing an organization's output mirrors its internal communication structure. The article closes with a practical culture checklist and a specific messaging framework for AI adoption: treat AI as just another tool great engineers learn to use, never frame it as replacement, and drive adoption bottom-up rather than top-down since forced adoption reliably backfires.
points: The author identifies a specific executive statement — 'this is very easy to build now that we have AI, and we don't need as many people' — as directly damaging to psychological safety and culture, especially when it comes from a CEO, CPO, or CTO.

Using Conway's Law, the piece argues that an organization's output quality mirrors its communication structure, so AI cannot fix a bad culture; instead 'AI makes bad communication even worse, it also makes bad architecture even worse as well,' amplifying whatever culture already exists.

Panic over competitors' reported '10x productivity' from AI tools is identified as a trap: much of that reporting is disguised vendor marketing, and CEOs who blame their own teams for not matching it actively damage trust and culture in the process.

The recommended AI-adoption messaging treats AI as just another tool great engineers have always adopted, explicitly avoiding any language of 'replacing' people, because adoption 'only works bottom-up, it never works top-down' given how fast the tools are changing.

The article reframes the central leadership question from 'how do we get everyone to use AI' to 'how do we build an organization where great people can do their best work, and then use AI to multiply them' — positioning AI adoption as fundamentally a leadership problem, not a tooling problem.
quotes: There is no better productivity hack than a great culture. No AI tools will provide bigger productivity gains.
If the culture is bad, the end product will be bad as well, because people just don't work together well and they don't communicate properly.
AI makes bad communication even worse, it also makes bad architecture even worse as well.
My recommendation: Always take a look at what the incentives are behind people saying something, that says a lot about whether it's true or not.
AI adoption is not a tooling problem, it's a leadership problem.

Don't ever mention something even close to "replacing" or something along the lines of "You are not important anymore, because we have AI". Those are just going to completely diminish morale and break the entire culture.
How do we build an organization where great people can do their best work, and then use AI to multiply them?
